nameStory: The name 'speedwell' comes from an old farewell blessing meaning 'God speed you well' or 'may you prosper on your journey.' These cheerful little flowers were traditionally given to travelers as a good luck charm, and their quick-blooming nature seemed to embody the wish for swift, safe travels.
description: Long-leaved Speedwell is a tall, upright perennial wildflower that can reach 2-4 feet in height. It produces dense, spike-like clusters of tiny blue or purple flowers that rise above narrow, lance-shaped leaves. This European native has escaped cultivation and naturalized in parts of New England, where it forms attractive clumps in gardens and disturbed areas. The plant has a sturdy, somewhat rigid appearance compared to its smaller speedwell cousins.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, tapering spikes of tiny blue to purple flowers, each about 1/4 inch across with four petals and prominent white stamens that stick out like tiny antennae

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, narrow leaves with serrated edges arranged in pairs up the stem, feeling slightly rough and textured when rubbed between your fingers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall and upright with multiple sturdy stems forming clumps, much taller than most other speedwells you'll encounter in New England

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square-ish stems that feel firm and slightly ridged when rolled between your fingers, often with a reddish tinge

habitat: Long-leaved Speedwell thrives in disturbed soils, roadsides, old garden sites, and field edges with good drainage. It prefers full sun to partial shade and tolerates poor soils well. You're most likely to find it near old homesteads, abandoned gardens, or areas where European settlers once lived, as it often persists long after cultivation ends.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges early with fresh green leaves, but flowers haven't appeared yet. Look for the characteristic narrow, serrated leaves in opposite pairs.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time from June through August, when the tall blue flower spikes are most prominent and easiest to identify from a distance.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules develop, while leaves may turn yellowish. The dried flower spikes often persist into early fall.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving only dried stems and seed heads that may persist through early winter before breaking down.

funFact: Long-leaved Speedwell is like a botanical time capsule - it often marks the locations of old New England homesteads and abandoned gardens, sometimes persisting for decades or even centuries after the original settlers moved on, earning it the nickname 'ghost garden flower' among some botanists.
confusionNotes: The tall flower spikes might be confused with Purple Loosestrife, but speedwell's flowers are much smaller and have four petals (not six), and the leaves are arranged in pairs rather than alternating up the stem. Remember: speedwell spells 'square stems and paired leaves.'
contextualKnowledge: This species is sometimes called 'Garden Speedwell' because it was originally brought to New England as an ornamental garden plant. Many speedwells you encounter will be much smaller, weedy species, so finding this tall, showy one often indicates you're near a site with European settlement history.
compareHints: Long-leaved Speedwell towers over most other New England speedwells - while species like Thyme-leaved Speedwell hug the ground and Germander Speedwell stays low in lawns, this species stands tall with substantial flower spikes. Its narrow, serrated leaves are also much longer than the small, rounded leaves typical of most speedwell species in our region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's speedwells, heath speedwell is unique for its distinctly creeping, mat-forming growth habit and very fuzzy stems and leaves.
Among New England's speedwells, thyme-leaved speedwell is unique in its strongly creeping, mat-forming habit - most other speedwells grow more upright.
Among the speedwells, germander speedwell stands out for having the brightest blue flowers and the most prominent flower stalks that clearly rise above the foliage.
Among the speedwells, corn speedwell is distinguished by its fuzzy leaves and very small size - it's one of the tiniest in the genus.
Among the speedwells, marsh speedwell is distinctive for its wetland habitat and very narrow leaves.
Bird's-eye speedwell stands out from its many speedwell relatives by having the brightest, most intensely blue flowers with the most prominent dark radiating lines.
Among the many speedwells in New England, American brooklime is the water-lover of the group.
Among New England's many speedwell species, purslane speedwell stands out for its highly variable leaf shapes on a single plant and its preference for the most disturbed habitats.
Unlike the upright thyme-leaved speedwell or the larger-flowered Germander speedwell, slender speedwell stays flat to the ground with its characteristic thread-thin stems.
Unlike most other New England speedwells that are annual weeds or die back completely in winter, creeping speedwell is a true perennial that forms permanent mats.

Among New England speedwells, broadleaf speedwell stands out for its relatively large, oval leaves and dense flower spikes - most other speedwells have much smaller, narrower leaves and more open flower arrangements.
Among New England's many speedwells, blue water-speedwell is unique in its aquatic lifestyle - while American brooklime also likes wet areas, it grows taller and has larger flowers.
Among New England's speedwells, ivy-leaved speedwell is easily distinguished by its distinctive lobed leaves that look like tiny ivy leaves.
Unlike its lowland speedwell relatives that grow in fields and gardens, American alpine speedwell is the mountain specialist of the family.
Spiked speedwell towers over its New England speedwell relatives, most of which are small, creeping, or prostrate plants with much smaller flower clusters.
Among the many speedwells in New England, Pink Ivy-leaved Speedwell stands out for its distinctly lobed, ivy-like leaves - most other speedwells have simple, unlobed leaves.
Grey field-speedwell stands out from its speedwell relatives primarily by its grayish leaf color and extremely small size.
Among the speedwells, chain speedwell is unique for its strong preference for aquatic habitats and its creeping, often floating growth habit.
